newsitem.title: GERMANY: U.S. proposes moves to assist NATO reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. proposes moves to assist NATO reforms.

text.p: The United States has tried to put new momentum into NATO's post-Cold War transformation by formally proposing that a NATO summit in 1997 should approve an alliance charter with Russia.
It has also signalled more explicitly than before its hope that NATO will admit new members from eastern Europe in the year 2000.

"Let me share with you the vision that President Clinton and I have for the United States and Europe in the year 2000. It is a vision for a 'New Atlantic Community'," U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher said in a major speech on Friday.
Christopher told German officials that the new Atlantic community would extend across Europe to Russia and deepen the U.S. partnership with a broader, more integrated Europe.
In Orlando, Florida, where he was campaigning for re-election, President Bill Clinton urged fellow NATO heads of government "to join with me in this endeavour."

"Together, we can make this summit the most historic and forward looking in the history of our NATO alliance, furthering our vision of an undivided Europe and building a bridge of peace and security, democracy and prosperity to the 21st century," he said in a statement.
Clinton's Republican presidential challenger, Bob Dole, has criticised him for not moving faster on NATO's expansion.

Christopher's address commemorated the 50th anniversary of the "speech of hope" delivered in Stuttgart by then secretary of state James Byrnes, who promised that the United States would help to re-integrate a democratic, unified Germany into Europe after World War Two.

"Byrnes' far-sighted approach set the stage for...the remarkable generation that led the recovery of Europe and gave us 50 years of peace and prosperity," said Christopher, saying he hoped to set a similar stage for the post-Cold War era.

Christopher made the first formal U.S. offer of a NATO charter with Russia and publicly made clear that Washington wanted a NATO summit next year to decide which countries from eastern Europe should be the first to join the alliance.
U.S. officials said some NATO members regarded this pace as too fast, but Christopher had consulted German, French and British leaders who were reported as agreeing with his approach.
Moscow has long opposed NATO plans to take in new members from ex-Warsaw Pact states. But U.S. officials said it was now intensely engaged in talks on a long-term Russia-NATO relationship.
"NATO's cooperation with Russia should be expressed in a formal charter," Christopher said. Officials said the document would set out "rules of the road" for cooperation in Europe.
The Czech Republic, Hungary and Poland are generally regarded as the front-runners to join NATO first when its expansion is agreed.
Christopher said talks should begin with other potential candidates once first new members were chosen and he proposed ways to strengthen NATO's "partnership for peace" programme.
Under a long-scheduled plan, NATO foreign ministers are to meet in Brussels in December to discuss the alliance's expansion eastward, internal reforms and ties with Russia.
U.S. officials said the meeting will not take decisions but would set the stage for a NATO summit somewhere in Europe in the first half of 1997.
